title: Banjo solos and reading on the boats; dance hall banjoists
summary: Banjo solos were expected on the boats, bands read music, and leaders in rougher dance bands often did not let banjos solo.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: On the riverboats there, you know, you still play the same stuff as you're playing today, that, you know, afterbeat stuff, and solo work, did you do solo work?
Banjo? Yeah. Oh, yes, I did. Yeah, I did a lot of solos, you know. At least, well, they didn't allow banjos too much, but you always had to have some of them with the solo on, you know. Mm-hmm.
And you sit there, and, well, they were most reading bands in those days, like on the boat especially, even the bands around, yeah. They had a lot of...
Because you've always been a reader. Huh? You've always been able to read.
Oh, yeah, yeah. I started out reading, yeah. Yeah.

How about the banjos in the old rougher type bands, you know, the dancehall bands like Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly in there? What did the banjo players in there, did they differ from your type of playing?

Well, each guy had his particular style and playing, you know. Some guys I know, probably they couldn't solo, but sometimes leaders, some leaders wouldn't even permit banjo to solos, you know. Like I said, those days I remember the solo number was well, waiting for the sunrise, and Tiger Rag, you know, that was a muscle and a banjo.
